section.title: Walk in Love and Light
section.sectionRationale: Paul continues the call to a worthy walk with three great pictures of the Christian life: walk in love, walk as children of light, and walk wisely, filled with the Spirit. The believer is to imitate God as a beloved child, loving as Christ loved and gave Himself, and to turn decisively from the sexual immorality, greed, and empty words that mark the darkness and bring the wrath of God. Once darkness themselves, believers are now light in the Lord, called to live out the fruit of the light and expose the deeds of darkness. The passage climaxes in the contrast between drunkenness and Spirit-filled worship, thanksgiving, and song.
section.thesis: As beloved children, believers are to imitate God by walking in the self-giving love of Christ, to turn wholly from the immorality and greed that belong to darkness and bring God's wrath, to live as children of light bearing its fruit of goodness, righteousness, and truth, and to walk wisely in evil days, not drunk with wine but filled with the Spirit in worship, song, and thanksgiving.
section.frameNote: Four movements: walk in love, imitating God as Christ loved us; turn from the works of darkness that bring God's wrath; walk as children of light, exposing and dispelling the darkness; and walk wisely, redeeming the time and filled with the Spirit.

units.label: Walk in love, imitating God
units.note: as Christ loved us and gave Himself

verses.text: Be {{mimetes|imitators}} of God, therefore, as beloved children,
and walk in {{agape|love}}, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial {{prosphora|offering}} to God.

units.label: Turn from the works of darkness
units.note: the wrath of God is coming

verses.text: But among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed.
Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving.
For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
Therefore do not be partakers with them.

units.label: Walk as children of light
units.note: the fruit of the light exposes the dark

verses.text: For you were once darkness, but now you are {{phos|light}} in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the {{karpos|fruit}} of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.
Test and prove what pleases the Lord.
Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.
For it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret.
But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.
So it is said: "Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you."

units.label: Walk wisely, filled with the Spirit
units.note: redeeming the time, singing to the Lord

verses.text: Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise,
{{exagorazo|redeeming}} the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord's will is.
Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be {{pleroo|filled}} with the Spirit.
Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord,
always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

mimetes.gloss: An imitator, one who mimics or copies a pattern, from which the English word mimic derives. Believers are to be imitators of God, copying His character as beloved children copy a father they love. The imitation is specific: to love as He loves, shown supremely in Christ's self-giving. Grace does not end in mere pardon but in a family likeness to God.

agape.gloss: Love, especially self-giving, sacrificial love that seeks the good of another at cost to oneself. It is the love God is and the love Christ displayed in giving Himself up for us. To walk in agape is to pattern one's whole life on this love, the opposite of the greed and impurity that use others; it is the defining mark of the imitator of God.

prosphora.gloss: An offering, a sacrifice presented to God. Paul describes Christ's self-giving as a fragrant offering, using the language of the Old Testament sacrifices whose smoke rose as a pleasing aroma to God. Christ's death is the true and final offering, freely given, that fulfills the sacrificial system and becomes the pattern of the self-giving love believers are to imitate.

phos.gloss: Light, both physical light and, figuratively, the realm of God's truth, holiness, and life. Believers were once darkness itself, but now they are light in the Lord, sharing in the character of God who is light. As light they bear its fruit, live openly, and expose the deeds of darkness, for light by its nature drives out the dark and makes things visible.

karpos.gloss: Fruit, the natural produce of a living thing. The fruit of the light is all goodness, righteousness, and truth, the visible product of a life joined to the Lord. As a healthy tree bears fruit in keeping with its nature, so those who are light in the Lord naturally bring forth goodness, in contrast to the fruitless, barren deeds of darkness.

exagorazo.gloss: To redeem, buy up, purchase out of the marketplace, make the most of an opportunity. Believers are to redeem the time, buying up every opportunity for good because the days are evil. The word pictures the wise use of limited, precious time, seizing each moment for the Lord's purposes rather than squandering it in the folly of the age.

pleroo.gloss: To fill, to make full, to be filled. Paul commands believers to be filled with the Spirit, using a present tense that implies an ongoing, repeated filling rather than a single event. Set against being filled with wine, the Spirit's filling controls and shapes the whole person, overflowing into worship, mutual song, thanksgiving, and a life ordered by the will of God.

basic.context: Paul spells out the worthy walk with three great images. First, walk in love: imitate God as dearly loved children, loving as Christ loved us and gave Himself up as a fragrant offering. Second, turn from the darkness: sexual immorality, impurity, greed, and empty, corrupting talk have no place among God's people and bring His wrath on the disobedient. Third, walk as children of light, for those once darkness are now light in the Lord, bearing the fruit of goodness, righteousness, and truth and exposing the deeds of darkness. Finally, walk wisely in evil days, not drunk with wine but filled with the Spirit, overflowing in song, thanksgiving, and worship.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage is built around the repeated call to walk: in love, as light, and in wisdom. Each walk has a contrast, love against lust and greed, light against darkness, Spirit-filled wisdom against drunken folly. Read the warnings about God's wrath in verses 5 and 6 as sober and real, and the command to be filled with the Spirit in verse 18 as the positive center: the Spirit-filled life produces the worship and thanksgiving that close the section.
basic.originalLanguages: Believers are to be mimetes, imitators, of God, walking in agape, self-giving love, after the pattern of Christ who gave Himself as a fragrant prosphora, offering, to God. Once darkness, they are now phos, light, in the Lord, bearing the karpos, fruit, of goodness, righteousness, and truth. They are to walk wisely, exagorazo, redeeming the time, and above all to be pleroo, filled, with the Spirit, overflowing in song and thanksgiving.
basic.typology: Christ's self-giving is described as a fragrant offering, fulfilling the Old Testament sacrifices whose smoke rose as a pleasing aroma to God. The whole system of offerings finds its true and final meaning in Christ, who gave Himself once for all. Believers, in turn, imitate this offering as they walk in the same self-giving love.
basic.christ: Christ is the pattern and power of the walk. He loved us and gave Himself up as a fragrant offering, the model of the love believers are to imitate. He is the Lord in whom the darkness becomes light, and the one who shines on those who wake from sleep, as verse 14 declares. The kingdom is His and God's, and every thanksgiving rises in His name. He is the light that dispels the dark and the love that shapes the new life.
basic.god: God is the Father whom His children imitate, whose very character is love and light. He is pleased by the fragrant offering of Christ and by the thanksgiving of His people. He is also holy and just: His wrath is coming on the sons of disobedience, and the immoral and greedy have no inheritance in His kingdom. The same God who is light calls His children to walk in the light and gives His Spirit to fill them.
basic.crossReferences: First John says God is light and calls us to walk in the light. Romans 13 urges casting off the works of darkness and putting on Christ. Colossians 3 gives the parallel call to sing psalms and hymns with thankfulness in the heart to God.
basic.oneStory: This passage carries the movement from darkness to light that runs through the whole Bible, from the first light spoken into the dark in Genesis to the Lord who shines on those raised from death. God is making His people light in a dark world, imitators of His love, a foretaste of the city that needs no sun because the glory of God is its light. The self-giving offering of Christ stands at the center, fulfilling the sacrifices and forming a people who walk in His love.

context.literary:
The paragraph is stitched together by the verb 'walk', which Paul has used since Ephesians 2:2 and now deploys three times in quick succession: walk in love, 5:2, walk as children of light, 5:8, and watch how you walk, 5:15. Between the first and second walk stands a negative section, verses 3 to 7, and between the second and third a quotation, verse 14, that sits like a hinge between light and wisdom. The section ends with a string of five participles, speaking, singing, making music, giving thanks and (in verse 21, the bridge to the next study) submitting, all hanging from the one command to be filled with the Spirit.

Within this frame the thought moves on a repeating pattern of 'once, but now'. 'You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.' The language of verse 8 is stronger than a comparison. The readers were not merely in darkness; they were darkness, and they are now light. The commands follow from that identity, as in the previous chapter.

Several pairs sharpen the contrasts. Impurity against thanksgiving in verse 4, drunkenness against Spirit-filling in verse 18, foolishness against understanding the Lord's will in verse 17, and the works of darkness against the 'fruit' of light in verses 9 and 11. Notice that the works of darkness are 'fruitless' while the light bears fruit. The paragraph begins with the Father and the Son, in verses 1 and 2, and ends with the Father and the Son again, in verse 20, so that the whole walk is framed by the God who is imitated and the God who is thanked.
context.historical:
Paul's readers lived in a city where heavy drinking, sexual licence and the pursuit of gain were embedded in public religion and private life. The Greek world knew festivals in honour of Dionysus where wine was drunk in the god's honour and drunkenness could pass for religious fervour, and Paul's contrast in verse 18 would have been heard against that background. The believer is also to be filled, but by the Spirit, and what flows out is not loose behaviour but a clear mind and shared song.

The sexual and greedy sins of verse 3 are named with an unusual severity. In a pagan setting they were often treated as private matters, but Paul says they must not even be 'named' among saints. Greed is linked to idolatry in verse 5, a connection the Old Testament also makes: the grasping heart has found a rival god. 'Obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking' reflects a culture in which sharp wit and bawdy humour were admired at banquets and public meetings, and Paul asks for a different atmosphere in the Christian gathering, one that overflows with thanksgiving.

The line in verse 14, 'Wake up, O sleeper', is introduced by 'it is said' and has no exact match in the Old Testament. Many suggest it is an early Christian hymn or baptismal chant, shaped by Isaiah 60:1, 'Arise, shine, for your light has come', and Isaiah 26:19. If so, it shows that the first churches sang the gospel, and that Paul is quoting a song his readers already knew. The command to sing psalms and hymns in verse 19 would then be something they were doing already.
context.canonical:
The call to imitate God as His children reaches back to Leviticus 19:2, 'Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy', and forward to Jesus' command to love enemies so as to be sons of the Father in heaven, Matthew 5:44 to 45 and 5:48. Paul's version places the pattern in Christ: He loved us and gave Himself. Jesus' own commandment, 'love one another as I have loved you', John 13:34, sits right behind the verse.

The 'fragrant offering' is language from the sacrificial law. The burnt offering is a 'pleasing aroma to the LORD', Leviticus 1:9, and the phrase reaches back as far as Noah's sacrifice, Genesis 8:21. Paul gives it a new object: Christ's self-giving on the cross. Hebrews 10:10 to 12 follows the same line, saying the sacrifice was offered once for all.

The light and darkness language runs through the Bible, from the first day of creation, Genesis 1:3, through Isaiah's promise of light for those in darkness, Isaiah 9:2, to Jesus' word that He is the light of the world, John 8:12, and His call to His followers to be the light of the world, Matthew 5:14. First John says that God is light and that to walk in the light is to have fellowship, 1 John 1:5 to 7. Paul himself draws on the same imagery in 1 Thessalonians 5:4 to 8, where believers are 'sons of light', and in Romans 13:11 to 14, where he too says it is time to wake from sleep.

The Spirit-filled life of verses 18 to 20 is paralleled in Colossians 3:16 to 17, where the word of Christ dwells richly, and the people sing and give thanks. Luke's writings show believers being filled with the Spirit, Acts 2:4 and 4:31, and the account of Pentecost carries a charge of drunkenness, Acts 2:13 to 15, a nice echo of Paul's contrast.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's purpose is to show that the Christian life has a character, and the character is that of God Himself. The opening command, 'be imitators of God', is startling, and he softens it only with the words 'as beloved children'. Children imitate a father because they are loved by him and want to be like him, not to earn his love. Paul wants the church to see its ethics as family likeness.

He also means to draw a firm line around the community. The sins of verses 3 to 5 are not discussed as moral puzzles but as things that have no place among those who have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. The warning is sober: the same wrath that falls on the disobedient will not turn aside because someone calls himself a believer, and empty words that excuse such behaviour are deception. Paul does not mean that the church is a place of fear, but that the stakes of discipleship are real.

Finally, he wants his readers to discover joy. The long list of things to avoid gives way to a picture of a congregation filled with the Spirit, singing, thanking, and living with a clear head. The target is not merely to refuse darkness but to become a source of light, 'exposing' it simply by shining. Paul's hope is for a people whose life together is attractive in itself, and whose worship is a daily thing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This paragraph is made almost wholly of commands, and the commands are for every believer. Be imitators of God, walk in love, avoid sexual immorality, impurity, greed, crude talk, do not be deceived by empty words, walk as children of light, make the most of the time, be filled with the Spirit, sing, give thanks. Nothing here needs to be turned from description into prescription; the whole is written to be done.

The more careful question is how to apply particular lines. 'Test and prove what pleases the Lord' makes the Christian a thinker, not merely a rule follower, and asks that decisions be weighed. 'Expose' in verse 11 does not tell believers to go hunting for faults in others; verse 12 says it is shameful even to mention what is done in secret, so exposure here is chiefly by contrast, the light shining on what it touches. 'Do not get drunk on wine' is a command against drunkenness, not a rule against any use of wine, and the comparison with the Spirit shows what is really at stake: what controls us.

The quoted hymn in verse 14 is neither a command nor a record of a historical event. It is a call to the spiritually asleep, and the believer who reads it is meant to hear it first as good news and then as an alarm clock for the drowsy.

debates.question: What does it mean to be 'filled with the Spirit' in verse 18?

views.label: A command to be controlled by the Spirit
views.case: The contrast with drunkenness suggests the Spirit should have the same kind of governing influence over the whole person that wine has over the drunk, yet with the opposite result, clear thinking and self control. The imperative is plural and present tense, so it is a command for the whole church, to be kept up.

views.label: A fresh filling distinct from the Spirit's indwelling
views.case: Some Pentecostal and charismatic traditions teach that this is an experience after conversion, an empowering for service like those recorded in Acts 2:4 and 4:31. On this view the present tense is a call to seek and repeat the experience.

views.label: The fullness of Christ's presence in the church
views.case: The verb used in Ephesians 3:19 and 4:13 is the same word, and there it concerns being filled with all the fullness of God and of Christ. The command then means the whole church is to live in the fullness of what it already has, with the Spirit as the one who fills.

debates.bearing: All agree the verse is addressed to all believers, in the present, and that the result is seen in worship, mutual speech, thanksgiving and humility, as the participles that follow show. The verse does not make a believer who feels no special experience second class; it asks all to depend on the Spirit continually.

debates.question: What is meant by 'redeeming the time' in verse 16?

views.label: Make the most of every opportunity
views.case: The common sense is to buy up time that is passing, to use each opening for good. The reason given, 'the days are evil', suggests that opportunities are fleeting and that the ungodly world will crowd them out.

views.label: Use wisdom to deal with a hostile age
views.case: Others stress the link with verse 15 and the call to wisdom, and read it as conducting oneself prudently in a hostile environment. The same phrase appears in Colossians 4:5, 'making the most of every opportunity' with outsiders, and the focus is on how to behave toward those who do not believe.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the believer's time is a gift to be used, and that evil days are not an excuse for passivity. The word for time here means a season or opportunity, not clock time, so the stress is on seizing moments, not on frantic activity.

study.originalLanguages:
The call to be imitators is built on mimetes, the root of our word 'mimic', but the New Testament uses it for following an example, not for simply copying. Paul calls on the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitates Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:1, and he commends the Thessalonians as imitators of the churches, 1 Thessalonians 1:6 and 2:14. In Ephesians 5:1 the only time believers are told to imitate God Himself, the pattern is given at once: 'walk in love', and the model is Christ's giving.

The warnings of verse 3 use three nouns, porneia, akatharsia and pleonexia. The first is a broad word for sexual immorality of every kind, the second means uncleanness, and the third literally means a wanting of more, the same word used in 4:19. Paul says these things must not even be 'named' among the saints, a way of saying they should not be spoken of as though they were acceptable. In verse 4 Paul names three kinds of speech: aischrotes, shameful or obscene talk, morologia, foolish talk, and eutrapelia, a word that began as praise for clever wit but here carries the sense of crude jesting. The positive opposite, eucharistia, thanksgiving, is the word later used for the Lord's Supper. The conversation of the saints is meant to be marked by gratitude.

Verse 5 says an idolater cannot have an inheritance, and the word for 'idolater' is eidololatres, which ties the sins of verse 3 to the worship of something other than God. The 'sons of disobedience' of verse 6 is a Hebrew way of speaking, 'sons of' meaning those marked by a trait; Paul has used it before in 2:2.

In verse 8 the Greek is blunt: 'you were darkness' and 'you are light', not 'in darkness' or 'in the light'. Verse 11 uses elencho, which can mean to expose, to convict or to reprove, and the same verb is used for the Spirit's work of convicting the world, John 16:8. Verse 13 turns on a participle that can be read either as 'everything exposed becomes visible' or as 'everything made visible becomes light', and the translators have taken the second.

The command in verse 15 uses akribos, 'carefully' or 'accurately', a word for exactness, and in verse 16 the word for time is kairos, an opportunity or season, not chronos. 'Redeeming', exagorazo, means to buy up, and Paul uses the same verb in Galatians 3:13 for Christ buying us out of the curse of the law. The command in verse 18, plerousthe, is a present imperative in the passive voice, 'keep on being filled', and the phrase 'in the Spirit' may be read as the means or the content of the filling. Verses 19 to 21 then give five participles, the first four describing what the filled life does: speaking, singing, making music and giving thanks. The three kinds of song, psalmoi, hymnoi and odai pneumatikai, appear again in Colossians 3:16.

typology.type: The pleasing aroma of the burnt offering
typology.fulfillment: In Leviticus 1:9 the burnt offering goes up entirely on the altar as 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD', and Noah's offering after the flood is received in the same way, Genesis 8:21. Paul says Christ gave Himself up 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering'. The correspondence is that a whole life is given up to God, but the escalation is that Christ's offering is willing, once for all and effective, Hebrews 10:10 to 14. Believers share in it by offering their own bodies, Romans 12:1, and the gifts they send, Philippians 4:18. The animal sacrifices were shadows and could not take away sin, Hebrews 10:4.

The first act of creation was God's word calling light into the dark, Genesis 1:3, and Paul uses the same picture for the conversion of a person, 2 Corinthians 4:6. Israel's exodus included a pillar of fire that lit the way, Exodus 13:21, and Isaiah promised light dawning on a people in darkness, Isaiah 9:2. Christ is the true light, John 1:9, who makes His people lights, Matthew 5:14. The picture is not complete in the present: the final light has no need of sun or lamp because God Himself is the light, Revelation 22:5.

typology.type: Waking from sleep and rising from the dead
typology.fulfillment: Verse 14 calls the sleeper to rise from the dead, and the text bears echoes of Isaiah's summons, 'Arise, shine', Isaiah 60:1, and the prophecy that the dead will rise, Isaiah 26:19. In Christ the dead are literally raised, as Lazarus was, John 11:43 to 44, and as Christ Himself was, 1 Corinthians 15:20. Believers have already been raised with Him spiritually, Ephesians 2:5 to 6, and will be raised bodily. The picture is partial, since sleep is a figure, whereas Paul elsewhere says plainly that the unbeliever is dead, Ephesians 2:1.

Old Testament prophecy anticipated a day when the Spirit would be poured out on all flesh, Joel 2:28. At Pentecost the crowd mistook the believers for people drunk on wine, Acts 2:13 to 17, and Peter pointed to Joel. Paul takes the comparison further: where wine produces loss of control, the Spirit produces a fullness that overflows in song and thanks. The Spirit does not remove the person's self control, since it is itself a fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22 to 23, and the comparison reaches its limit there.

study.christ:
Christ stands at the beginning, the middle and the end of this passage. At the beginning He is the pattern: 'just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us'. Paul often grounds his ethics in the cross, and here he does so with a pair of verbs, loved and gave. The phrase 'gave Himself up' is the language used in Galatians 2:20, 'who loved me and gave Himself for me', and in Ephesians 5:25, where the husband is told to follow the same pattern. It was a willing act; no one took His life from Him, John 10:18.

In the middle He is the light. 'You are light in the Lord' means that the light is derived from union with Him. Jesus said, 'I am the light of the world', John 8:12, and He told His followers they were the light of the world, Matthew 5:14. Both are true because the second depends on the first. The hymn of verse 14 ends with the promise that 'Christ will shine on you'. In the gospel, the Lord who rose from the dead shines on those who were dead and gives them life, as Paul himself found on the road to Damascus, Acts 9:3 to 5.

The offering is a clear point of connection with the Old Testament sacrifices. Hebrews argues at length that the repeated sacrifices could not take away sin, and that Christ by one offering has made perfect those who are being made holy, Hebrews 10:10 to 14. Here the point is applied: the cross is the model of love, and the cost of the love is the offering of Himself. Love of this kind is not sentiment but the giving of oneself for the good of another.

At the end, the thanksgiving is offered 'in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ'. He is the one through whom believers come to the Father, John 14:6 and Ephesians 2:18, and the whole of the worship described in verses 19 and 20 is offered through Him. The kingdom that the immoral cannot inherit is 'the kingdom of Christ and of God', a phrase that places Christ and God together as sharing one rule.

Care is needed in the use of the pattern. Paul does not say, 'Love well and you will be accepted.' The order is that Christ has loved and given Himself, and now His people walk in that love. The imitation of Christ is the fruit of being loved by Him, not the price of it. The passage also warns against forgetting that Christ is not only example but the one who bears the wrath that is coming on the sons of disobedience, as 1 Thessalonians 1:10 says.
study.god:
The passage opens with God as Father, and the first thing it says about Him is that He has children who are beloved. Everything else is built on that. The ethics Paul asks for are the ethics of a household that carries the family likeness, and the model is God's own character, which Paul sums up as love shown in giving.

God is also light. In verse 8 the believers are light 'in the Lord', not in themselves, because He is the source. The apostle John says that God is light and in Him is no darkness at all, 1 John 1:5, and the psalmist says that with God is the fountain of life and that in His light we see light, Psalm 36:9. To live in the light is to be where God's character is on display, and to bear the fruit of goodness, righteousness and truth, which describe Him.

The passage is also clear that God is just. Verse 6 speaks of a coming wrath, and verse 5 bars the idolatrous from any inheritance. Paul does not soften this, and he does not set it against love. Because God is loving, He cannot be indifferent to what destroys the people He loves. The fragrant offering of verse 2 is the way in which both are held together: the wrath is real, and Christ's love has met it.

The God of this passage is pleased. Both the offering of Christ and the thanksgiving of His people are pleasing to Him. Paul's command in verse 10 to find out what pleases the Lord assumes that God's pleasure can be known and that it matters. God is not distant or indifferent to the daily choices of His people; He is the one who watches and delights.

The Spirit is at work in the believer's worship. The filling of the Spirit produces song and thanks addressed to the Father in the name of the Son, so that the three persons are each named in the closing sentence. The whole of true worship is Trinitarian: from the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father.

For worship, the passage teaches that thanksgiving belongs at the centre of the church's life, not at the edge. Paul asks for thanks 'always' and 'for everything', which means the believer is asked to trust that the God who gave His Son is also in control of the details. A congregation marked by gratitude displays God's character better than any sermon on morals.

crossReferences.note: God tells Israel to be holy because He is holy. It is the Old Testament counterpart of Paul's command to imitate God, and it shows that the call to be like God is not a New Testament novelty but the basic shape of covenant life.

The burnt offering is 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD', and the phrase is the source of Paul's 'fragrant offering' in verse 2. The reader is meant to see Christ's death as the true sacrifice that the animal offerings only anticipated.

God is light with no darkness, and those who walk in the light have fellowship with one another and are cleansed by the blood of Jesus. It runs parallel with Ephesians 5:8 to 11, joining the call to the light with the cleansing of the cross.

Paul urges Christians to wake from sleep because salvation is nearer than when they first believed. They are to put aside the deeds of darkness and put on Christ. It is the same call as the hymn of verse 14 and the same shape of urgency.

'Arise, shine, for your light has come.' The prophet speaks to Zion, whose light is the glory of the LORD. The hymn in verse 14 echoes it, and the church is cast as the new Zion that shines with the glory of Christ.

The parallel to verses 19 and 20. The word of Christ dwells richly, believers teach and admonish one another with psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, and give thanks to the Father through Him. It shows that Spirit filling and the word of Christ are two sides of one life.

Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, which includes self-control. It shows that the Spirit-filled life of Ephesians 5:18 is marked by character, and not simply by feelings.

On the day of Pentecost the crowd thought the believers were full of new wine, and Peter answered that it was the outpouring of the Spirit promised by Joel. It is the closest narrative parallel to the contrast Paul draws in verse 18.

Jesus tells His disciples they are the light of the world and are to let their light shine so that others may see their good works and glorify the Father. It gives the practical purpose of walking as children of light.

Paul describes the gift sent by the Philippians as a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God. It shows that the picture of the sweet aroma extends from Christ's offering to the lives and gifts of His people.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with light spoken into darkness, Genesis 1:3, and with humanity made in the likeness of God to reflect His character in the world. Sin breaks that likeness and plunges people into the darkness described in Ephesians 5. The sins named in verses 3 to 5, sexual disorder and grasping greed, are the same distortions that have marked fallen humanity since the garden: appetite ruling where trust should rule, and the creature grasping what belongs to the Creator.

Israel's story added a pattern for the answer. God called Abraham so that all families of the earth might be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and Israel was to be a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6. They often failed, and the prophets looked ahead to a servant who would be the light that Israel was not. In Christ that servant came, and the apostles took Isaiah's words as their commission, Acts 13:47. Ephesians 5 shows the result: a community of former Gentiles, once darkness, now light in the Lord, whose life is meant to draw others toward Him.

The offering of Christ at the centre of the passage is where the story turns. The sacrificial system had taught Israel that sin was serious and that approach to God was costly. Christ's self-giving fulfilled it, and so the people He purchased could be called saints, with an inheritance in the kingdom. The Spirit, promised for the last days in Joel 2:28, fills them, and the Spirit's fruit is a people who sing and give thanks.

There is a note of urgency because the days are evil. The story is not yet finished, and the church lives in a dark age with a light that is real but not yet complete. Paul's call to wake from sleep belongs to the same awareness as Romans 13:11 to 12, that the night is far gone and the day is at hand.

The end of the story is a city with no need of the sun, since the glory of God gives it light, and the nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:23 to 24. The darkness is gone, nothing impure will enter, and the people of God worship before the throne, Revelation 22:3 to 5. The songs of Ephesians 5:19 anticipate the songs of that city. What is a hymn in a house church now will be the sound of the whole creation then.

quiz.q: What does it mean to be imitators of God in verses 1 and 2?

options.text: To walk in self-giving love as beloved children, as Christ loved and gave Himself.
options.note: Imitating God means loving as He loves, shown in Christ's self-giving.

options.text: To try to become divine and equal with God.
options.note: The call is to copy God's love as His children, not to become God.

options.text: To imitate His power rather than His character.
options.note: The imitation Paul names is love, His character, patterned on Christ's sacrifice.

options.text: To keep rules while ignoring love.
options.note: The heart of the imitation is walking in love.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call greed idolatry in verse 5?

options.text: Because the greedy person sets created things in the place that belongs to God.
options.note: Greed makes an idol of possessions and desire, so no idolater inherits the kingdom.

options.text: Because money itself is inherently evil.
options.note: The issue is the greedy heart that idolizes, not that possessions are evil in themselves.

options.text: Because greed is only a minor social flaw.
options.note: Paul treats it as idolatry that excludes from the kingdom, not a minor flaw.

options.text: Because generosity is forbidden to believers.
options.note: Paul commends thanksgiving and generosity; he condemns greed as idolatry.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the change in believers in verse 8?

options.text: Once they were darkness, but now they are light in the Lord.
options.note: Believers do not merely see light; they have become light in the Lord.

options.text: They were always partly light and only needed polishing.
options.note: Paul says they were once darkness itself, now light in the Lord.

options.text: They remain in darkness but try to act better.
options.note: The change is real: they are now light and are to walk as children of light.

options.text: They became light by their own effort apart from the Lord.
options.note: They are light in the Lord, by His work, not their own.

quiz.q: What is the fruit of the light according to verse 9?

options.text: All goodness, righteousness, and truth.
options.note: The light naturally produces goodness, righteousness, and truth.

options.text: Wealth, comfort, and worldly success.
options.note: The fruit is moral and spiritual, not material success.

options.text: Secret knowledge hidden from others.
options.note: The fruit is open goodness and truth, not secret knowledge.

options.text: Nothing visible at all.
options.note: The fruit is visible goodness, righteousness, and truth.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by redeeming the time in verse 16?

options.text: Making the most of every opportunity because the days are evil.
options.note: To redeem the time is to buy up each opportunity for good in an evil age.

options.text: Trying to relive and undo the past.
options.note: The call is to use present opportunities wisely, not to relive the past.

options.text: Filling every moment with busyness for its own sake.
options.note: It is wise, purposeful use of time for the Lord, not mere busyness.

options.text: Ignoring time since the days are evil anyway.
options.note: The evil of the days is the reason to use time wisely, not to waste it.

quiz.q: What contrast does Paul draw in verse 18?

options.text: Do not get drunk on wine, but be filled with the Spirit.
options.note: The Spirit, not wine, is to fill and control the believer.

options.text: Do not drink at all, and avoid all singing.
options.note: The contrast is drunkenness versus Spirit-filling, and it leads to singing.

options.text: Be filled with the Spirit only on special occasions.
options.note: The present tense implies an ongoing, continual filling, not occasional.

options.text: Rely on wine to loosen worship.
options.note: Paul opposes drunkenness; the Spirit produces true worship.

questions: Paul says to imitate God as beloved children. Where in your relationships is God calling you to love in the self-giving way Christ loved you?
There must not be even a hint of immorality or greed among the saints. Is there an area where you have been tolerating a hint of what belongs to the darkness?
You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. How does seeing yourself as light, not just as forgiven, change how you live in front of others?
The days are evil, so Paul urges redeeming the time. What is one opportunity for good God may be giving you that you could seize this week?
Paul contrasts being controlled by wine with being filled with the Spirit. What tends to fill and control you, and what would it look like to be filled with the Spirit instead?
Spirit-filled life overflows in song and thanksgiving for everything. What could you give thanks to God for today, even in the middle of a hard season?

translationNotes.note: A fragrant sacrificial offering uses the Old Testament language of a pleasing aroma rising to God from the sacrifices, applied to Christ's self-giving on the cross as the true and final offering.
That is, an idolater identifies the greedy person as an idolater, because greed sets created things in the place of God; the phrase explains why such a person has no inheritance in the kingdom.

So it is said introduces a quoted couplet, likely an early Christian hymn drawing on Isaiah's call to awake and arise; it is kept with straight double quotes and applied to Christ shining on those raised from spiritual death.
